column2: ENGLISH

[From.GetTitledFirstName] meets you at the bridge over the chasm, where the wards cut into the stone glow as you cross. Half the doors in the Guildhall are carved into the rock and lead nowhere. [From.GetFirstName] walks past them without a glance.\n\n"So you would be one of the Clan of Morgrim. Hear it plainly. Nothing we teach is written down. Not one rune, not ever. What Thungni taught his seven apprentices has come down to us mouth to ear, master to apprentice, and so it will go on. You will keep the Rules of Three, of Form, of Jealousy and of Pride, or you will answer to the Order of Hrungil. Swear it."
I swear it on my ancestors.

The Guild says a runesmith is only half a runesmith until he works at his own anvil, in his own forge. No runesmith strikes a rune on another's anvil, for the anvil is the mind of the forge, and it learns the hand that works it.\n\nThe masons are waiting for word, and the first fifty crowns have already left your coffers.
Cut the first stone.
Not yet. Give me back my gold.

Where to cut the forge? A forge deep in the hold is close at hand and hard to find, but the tunnels are close and smoke has nowhere to go. The forge quarter has room, good air and every smith in the hold watching what you do. Further off there is a sea cave the old clans used, and below the lowest halls the mountain's roots, where the rock is warm and no one comes.
Deep in the hold.
The forge is §Yhidden§!: rivals will struggle to find it, but a fire there spreads to the halls around it.
In the forge quarter, with the other smiths.
The forge is §Yopen§!: a §Gbetter forge§!, but anyone can find it.
In the old sea cave.
The forge is cut §Ydeep and far§!: §Groomy§! and very hard to find.
In the roots of the mountain.

The masons ask how great a forge you want. A single fire and anvil will do for a smith who works alone. A great forge, with its own furnaces and rune-hall, is the work of years and the talk of the hold. The greatest are spoken of like the Anvil Forge itself, the heart of a hold.\n\nThe greater the forge, the more it costs and the more there is to fit it out.
One fire, one anvil.
A §Ysmall§! forge: cheap and quick, with little to fit out.
A sound working forge.
A §Ysound§! forge: a fair start with more to fit out.
A great forge.
A §Ygreat§! forge: costly, with much to fit out.
A forge worthy of the ancestors.
A forge §Yworthy of the ancestors§!: very costly, and every fitting must be made.

Now the anvil, the Grong. You will forge it yourself, as every runesmith has since Thungni. It is the one thing in the forge no one may make for you. Plain iron is honest and will serve. An anvil faced with gromril will outlast your grandsons' grandsons, and the ore for it is not cheap.
Plain iron.
A §Yplain§! anvil.
Face it with gromril.
A §Ggromril-faced§! anvil: a finer forge, at a higher price.

The furnace. A charcoal furnace with good bellows is what most clan smiths have, and it is enough. Or you can have the miners sink a shaft to the deep heat of the mountain, as the old forges had, where the fire never has to be fed and burns all year except the two days before Zagazdeg.
Charcoal and bellows.
A §Yplain§! furnace.
Sink the shaft to the deep fire.
A §Gdeep-fire§! furnace: a finer forge, at a higher price.

Hammers and chisels. The clan smiths will make you a fine set of Grund and Klinka, new and true. But a trader has come to court with a chest of tools of old make, from a clan that died out when its hold fell. Each one is marked with a smith's sign no one living knows.
Good clan work.
§Yplain§! tools.
The old tools. Buy the chest.
§Gold-make§! tools: a finer forge, at a higher price.

The Guild writes nothing down, but a forge still needs its stones: slabs struck with the Klinkarun, the common runes an apprentice practises on, and a wall to cut the forge's grudges into, so that no wrong done to it is forgotten. You can cut them with your own chisel over many long nights, or pay a runescribe of the hold to do it well and quickly.
I will cut them myself.
§Yplain§! rune tablets.
Pay a runescribe.
§Gfine§! rune tablets: a finer forge, at a higher price.

The forge is finished. It is small and the smoke stings the eyes, and a passing smith from the forge quarter called it a cupboard with a fire in it. But the anvil is yours and the fire is lit, and that is what makes a runesmith.
It will do.
Humble Forge
This runesmith works in a small forge of his own.
The forge is finished: a sound, honest forge, with a good anvil and a fire that draws well. The old smiths who come to look at it nod and say little, which from them is praise.
Good work, well done.
Sound Forge
This runesmith works in a sound forge of his own.

The forge is finished, and it is a fine one. Two furnaces, an anvil that rings true, a wall for its grudges and room for an apprentice. The clan smiths come to see it and go away muttering about how some runesmiths think they are Runelords already.
Let them mutter.
Fine Forge
This runesmith works in a fine forge of his own.
A Great Forge

The forge is finished and the whole hold has come to see it. The furnaces stand around the anvil like the six furnaces around Kenaz in Karak Norn, the rune tablets cover a wall, and the grudge wall waits, still clean, for its first entry. Old runesmiths run their hands over the anvil and ask who forged it.\n\nThis is a forge that will be spoken of.
Light the furnaces.
Great Forge
This runesmith works in a great forge, spoken of across the hold.
A Forge the Ancestors Would Know

It is done. The furnaces burn on the mountain's own heat, the anvil is faced with gromril, the tools are of old make and the rune tablets were cut by masters. When the fire is first lit the anvil gives one deep note, and the old Runelord who came to bless it goes quiet for a long time.\n\n"I have heard that sound once before," he says at last. "In Karak Kadrin, at the Anvil Forge. Grungni himself would not be ashamed to work here."
Then let the work begin.
A Forge of the Ancestors
This runesmith works in a forge worthy of the ancestors, the pride of the hold.

Krunk! A badly banked fire got loose in the night and ran through the half-built forge. The timbers are ash and the stones are cracked. Where the forge is cut deep in the hold, the fire spread into the halls around it, and [runesmith_burned_courtier.GetFirstName] was caught in the smoke and pulled out badly burned.
Clear the ash and build on.
This time, iron doors and fire wards.
Spend a little more to keep the next fire from doing as much harm.

The jewelsmiths and the clan smiths have taken against your new forge. It is too big, they say, too proud, and it takes ore and miners the hold needs. Their apprentices have been picking fights with your masons in the ale halls, and the Guild masters have been asked to look into it.
Smaller plans and a barrel of ale for the guilds.
A §Ysmaller§! forge, but the guilds are content.
Let them grumble. It is my forge.
Damp from the new workings has got into your store, and a pot of rune salve has gone to a grey crust that would ruin any rune it touched.
Save what can be saved.
Build a proper dry store, whatever it costs.

[From.GetTitledFirstName] finds you at the ale bench. "You work on a borrowed fire and a borrowed anvil, [Root.GetFirstName], and you call yourself a runesmith. The Guild has noticed, and so have I. Cut yourself a forge and forge your own anvil, or stop wearing the apron."

Your apprentice [From.GetFirstName] works up the courage to speak. "Master, the other apprentices laugh at me. They say my master has no forge of his own, and that a runesmith without an anvil is like a dwarf without a beard. Will you not build one?"
Word reaches the Guild that your forge is lit. It is not much to look at, the masters say, but it is yours, and you have done what was asked.
Word reaches the Guild that your forge is lit, and it is a fine one. The masters speak of it at the Runemoot, and more than one asks if there is room in it for a second anvil.
Let them come and see.
Build a Forge
A runesmith needs a forge of his own and an anvil no one else has worked.
Take the §YBuild a Forge§! decision and see the work through to the end.

[From.GetTitledFirstName] speaks to you after the Guild meeting. "You are getting on, [Root.GetFirstName]. What you know, you know only because a master spoke it into your ear, and it will die with you unless you do the same. Take an apprentice. Give him the apron. That is the duty of every one of us."

A young kinsman of your clan, [From.GetFirstName], has been brought to court. The old ones say he has the gift: he can hear a flaw in a blade when it is struck, and he sat for a whole night once watching a runesmith work without saying a word. His father would see him take the apron, if you will have him.
Give him the apron.
Not this one.
You will have to find an apprentice yourself.

[From.GetFirstName] kneels in your forge in a new leather apron that still smells of the tanner, and swears the oaths of the apprentice: to keep the lore unwritten, to tell no one outside the Guild what he learns, and to serve his master until he forges an anvil of his own.
Then let us begin. Hold the tongs.

Your apprentice [From.GetFirstName] has forged his own anvil. You watched him strike the last rune into it, and you could not have done it better at his age. By the old law he can no longer work at yours. He bows, gathers his tools and goes to light a forge of his own.
Go. Do me proud.
Your apprentice [From.GetFirstName] is dead. He had the gift, and the lore you spoke into his ear is lost with him. You find you cannot work at the anvil for some days.
Your apprentice [From.GetFirstName] is dead. You find you do not mourn him greatly. Some apprentices were never going to forge their own anvil.
Cut his name on the forge wall.
Take an Apprentice
A runesmith must pass the lore on, mouth to ear, to an apprentice.
Name a courtier your §YRunesmith's Apprentice§!. If you don't, a candidate may come to you.

[From.GetTitledFirstName] lowers his voice. "Much of the lore was lost when the holds fell in the Time of Woe. Whole clans of runesmiths died with what they knew still in their heads. But not everything was in their heads. Some of it was struck into stone, and some of that stone is still down there. I know where to look. I need someone with the coin to pay for the looking."

A letter from [From.GetTitledFirstName], sealed with the Guild's mark:\n\n"I have three places for you. There are old workings in [ruin_site.GetName], dug by a clan long gone, where rune tablets were cut and left. There is a shrine of the ancestors at [temple_site.GetName] with a slab beneath it that no one has lifted in a thousand years. And there are the Guild's own tally-halls, where the counts of every rune ever struck are kept, if you have the patience for them. Choose, and send the coin."

A letter from [From.GetTitledFirstName], sealed with the Guild's mark and then sealed again:

"I have found it. A map, drawn by a ranger who came out of one of the fallen holds alive, to the rune-vault of its Runelord. The way is long and the halls are full of grobi and worse, and it will cost a great deal. But a vault like that may hold a master rune of the ancestors themselves.

If that is too rich for you, there are other places: old workings in [ruin_site.GetName], the shrine at [temple_site.GetName], or the Guild's tally-halls. Choose."
The lost hold. Whatever it costs.
A great cost and a great risk, but the vault may hold §Ya master rune of the ancestors§!.
If the search succeeds:
The old workings in [ruin_site.GetName].
A long way off and costly, but there may be rune tablets, or even §Ya finished rune§!.
The shrine at [temple_site.GetName].
Close to home and cheap, with a fair chance of something worth finding.
The tally-halls. It costs nothing but time.
Safe and free, but there is little to find.
The Rune-Vault

Three weeks below the earth. Two of the hired hammerers did not come back, and you will hear the grobi drums in your sleep for a long time. But at the end of the map there was a door with the Runelord's mark on it, still sealed, and behind the door, on an anvil cold for a thousand years, a master rune of the ancestors.\n\nYou hold it in your hands. The Gromthi made this. You are the first dwarf to touch it since they did.
It comes home with me.

In the old workings in [ruin_site.GetName] you find what you came for: a row of rune tablets, half buried in fallen rock, struck by a smith whose mark no one living knows. Some of the runes on them you have never seen. They are going home with you, every one.
The Guild must see these.

With the priests' leave you lift the slab under the shrine at [temple_site.GetName]. Beneath it is a second slab, struck with runes in an older hand, and a rune of warding that has held for a thousand years and lets go only when you speak the right name to it.
The ancestors left this for us.

Weeks in the tally-halls among the counts of runes struck and the names of the smiths who struck them. Most of it is what you knew already. But in the tally of one smith, dead six hundred years, there is a rune struck only once, and a note of what it was struck into. Now you know where to look.
It was worth the dust.

Kruk. The map was wrong. The passage it showed had fallen in long ago, and the way round it led to a flooded hall and nothing else. You come home with nothing to show for the coin and the dead. [From.GetFirstName] says the map was good when he bought it. You wonder who he bought it from, and how much he kept for himself.

Kruk. The old workings in [ruin_site.GetName] have been stripped. Someone was here before you, and not long ago: there are fresh marks where the tablets were prised out of the wall. Umgi, by the look of it, or worse.
Kruk. There is nothing under the slab at the shrine but older slab, and the priests are angry that you lifted it.
Kruk. Weeks in the tally-halls, and nothing in the counts you did not know. Your eyes ache and your beard is grey with dust.

Deep in the old workings in [ruin_site.GetName], in a hollow cut into the rock and sealed with a single rune, you find a finished rune: struck, bound and never used, as if its smith meant to come back for it. He never did.
I will finish what he began.
Recover Lost Rune Lore
Rune lore lost in the Time of Woe waits in old workings, shrines and fallen holds.
Pay for the search when the letter comes, and choose where to look.

[From.GetTitledFirstName] has a grudge against [infiltration_target.GetTitledFirstName], an old one, written down. "Their forge is full of secrets that ought to be shared," [From.GetFirstName] says, "and full of ore they did not earn. Help me get in, and we split what we find."

[From.GetTitledFirstName] has noticed you have no love for [infiltration_target.GetTitledFirstName] either. "Nor have I. Their forge is barely guarded and full of things a better smith could use. Help me get in."

[From.GetTitledFirstName] has been watching the forge of [infiltration_target.GetTitledFirstName]. "More runes in there than one smith can use in a lifetime. And more gold. Help me get in, and we split it."
[From.GetFirstName] sends word: the forge of [infiltration_target.GetFirstName] is cut somewhere deep and far, and the spies have not found the way to it yet. They need more time.
Tell them to keep looking.
The spies keep looking for the forge.

The spies found it at last: a forge cut so deep you can feel the mountain's heat through your boots. Two forge-wardens sit at the door with their axes across their knees and a keg of ale between them, sworn to search anyone who comes in.

The spies found the forge, hidden deep in the hold behind a door made to look like rock. Two forge-wardens sit at the door with their axes across their knees and a keg of ale between them, sworn to search anyone who comes in.
The forge stands in the forge quarter for anyone to see. Two forge-wardens sit at the door with their axes across their knees and a keg of ale between them, sworn to search anyone who comes in.
Every warden has a price.
The wardens will take the coin and look the other way.
A drop of rune salve in the keg.
If they drink it, they sleep. If they don't...
If it works:
If it fails:
[infiltration_companion.GetFirstName] picks a quarrel with them at the door.
While the wardens deal with [infiltration_companion.GetFirstName], you slip in alone.
This was a mistake. Go home.
The raid is off.
The wardens count their coin and do not look up as you pass. Inside, the forge is dark and the fire is banked low.
The wardens are snoring over the keg. Inside, the forge is dark and the fire is banked low.
You break things, I take things.
Split up: quicker, but alone.
I break things, you take things.
We take what we can, together.
Stay together: safer, but slower.
We wreck the place, together.
The wardens drain the keg to the last drop, belch, and go on sitting there with their axes across their knees. Dwarf heads are hard, and dwarf bellies harder. The raid is off.
Wazzock. I should have used two drops.
[infiltration_companion.GetFirstName] goes up to the wardens and calls their grandmothers beardless. In a moment all three of them are rolling in the dust of the passage. Nobody sees you go in.
Go for the rune-chest.
Go for the anvil.
[infiltration_companion.GetFirstName]'s insult is so feeble that the wardens just laugh, and go on laughing, and do not move from the door. The raid is off.
I am never taking [infiltration_companion.GetFirstName] anywhere again.
The noise wakes the wardens. They catch you with a hammer in your hand over a broken furnace, and drag you off to their master's cells.
You are caught red-handed. Someone has raised the alarm, and the wardens are on you before you can run. They drag you off to their master's cells.
The wardens wake as you are lifting the lid of the rune-chest. They drag you off to their master's cells.
The wardens were not fooled for long, and you were still inside when they came back. They drag you off to their master's cells.
Krunk.
Your wardens have caught [From.GetTitledFirstName] in your forge, a hammer or a lid in hand. In the old days you could have had a thief's hands. Now you can only ask what freedom is worth to them.
Their secrets, for their freedom.
If [From.GetFirstName] will not talk, they stay where they are.
Let them rot.
[From.GetTitledFirstName] comes down to your cell. "Tell me the runes you know that I don't, and you can go. Keep them, and you can stay here until you forget them."
Very well. I will talk.
I will die before I break the Rule of Jealousy.
You stay in the cell.
[From.GetFirstName] talks. Some of it may even be true. You let the thief go.
A grudge settled, of a kind.
[From.GetFirstName] will not say a word. At least the thief knows how to keep a secret.
Then rot.
[From.GetFirstName] has no use for you. You will stay in this cell until someone pays for you, or until you die.
Grungni, give me patience.
The rune-chest is not even locked. Inside, wrapped in oiled leather, there is a finished rune and a whole store of salve and ore besides.
The rune-chest is locked, but the store is not: ore and salve enough to keep a forge going for a year.
The rune-chest is locked with a rune you cannot break, and the store is empty. There is a purse of coin on the bench.
Take it and go.
You take a §Yrune§! from the chest.
You take a store of §Yore and salve§!.
Coin will have to do.

Someone has been in your forge. The rune-chest is open and a rune is gone, and the store with it. Your wardens swear they saw nothing, but the dust on the floor shows the boot prints of [From.GetTitledFirstName].
Someone has been in your forge. Your store of ore and salve is gone, and the dust shows the boot prints of [From.GetTitledFirstName].
Someone has been in your forge and taken the purse from the bench. The dust shows the boot prints of [From.GetTitledFirstName].
You take a hammer to everything: the furnaces, the bellows, the tablets on the wall, and last of all the anvil itself, until it cracks. No one will strike a rune in this forge again.
You smash what you can before you hear the wardens stir: the bellows, a furnace, a shelf of tools. It will be months before this forge works again.
You raise the hammer over the anvil, and the rune-ward cut into its side wakes. Its owner did not trust his wardens.
Done. Now run.
Grimnir...

Your forge is ruined. The furnaces are broken, the tablets smashed and the anvil cracked through. The dust shows the boot prints of [From.GetTitledFirstName]. The grudge goes into the wall first, before anything is mended.
Someone has been in your forge with a hammer. The bellows are torn and a furnace is broken, and the dust shows the boot prints of [From.GetTitledFirstName].
Your wardens find [From.GetTitledFirstName] dead at your anvil, hammer in hand. The rune-ward has done its work.
Let the ward be blessed.
[From.GetFirstName] comes back with a sack over each shoulder: ore and salve, and a good deal of it.
[From.GetFirstName] comes back with very little. The store was nearly empty.
Good. Now we split it.
You gain runic §Ymetals§!.
[From.GetFirstName] comes back covered in soot and grinning. "They will not light that forge again this year."
Good work.
You hear a flash and a scream from inside the forge. [From.GetFirstName] has found the rune-ward on the anvil. There is no time to go back for the body.
Run.
You and [From.GetFirstName] are away clean, through the passages and out into the forge quarter before the wardens know anything has happened.
This calls for a gorog.
Raid a Rival's Forge
A rival's forge holds runes and stores that ought to be yours.
Wait for word from your accomplice, then get past the forge-wardens.

A Runelord does not stop learning when he has his own anvil. Some go down to the oldest tablets in the hold and learn what the Gromthi knew. Some give their lives to the hammer and the rune chant, striking the same rune ten thousand times until it is as true as any rune ever struck. And some turn to the ancestors themselves, to Valaya and Grimnir and Grungni, whose anvils each have their own purpose.
The old tablets.
Follow the §YScholar§!'s path through the oldest lore.
The hammer and the chant.
Follow the §YMystic§!'s path of practice at the anvil.
The ancestors.
Follow the §YTheologian§!'s path to the ancestors.
Not yet.
You have spent years on the path of the old tablets. Lately the tablets seem to say less to you than they did.
You have spent years at the anvil, striking and chanting. Lately the hammer feels heavy in a way it never did.
You have spent years with the ancestors. Lately they have been quiet.
Back to the old tablets.
Back to the hammer and the chant.
To the ancestors.
I will keep to my path.

The oldest tablets of the hold are kept in the Guild's vaults, behind doors only the Runelords may open, and the keepers take a fee from anyone else. Or there are the old smiths in the ale halls, Full Beards who were apprentices before your grandfather was born, who will tell you what they remember for a mug of Grizdal.
Down to the vaults.
You already have leave to enter the vaults.
Pay the keepers for leave to enter the vaults, once and for good.
To the old smiths.
Months among the tablets, and the old smiths' stories. Runes that were only names to you now have shapes, and you know why the Rule of Three is the Rule of Three.
There is always more to learn.
Delver in Old Lore
This runesmith has spent months with the oldest tablets of the hold.

There are two ways to learn a rune by heart. You can strike it into iron again and again until your hand knows it better than your head. Or you can sit with the old chants, the ones the runesmiths sing as they work, until you know each rune by its sound.
At the anvil.
With the chants.
A season of it, from the first bell to the last. When you strike a rune now, you no longer think about it. You hear it ring before the hammer falls.
Again.
Rune after Rune
This runesmith has spent a season striking runes at the anvil.
The Rune Chants
This runesmith has learned the old rune chants by heart.

Each ancestor's anvil has its own purpose. Valaya's is learning and the home, the hearth fire and the warding rune. Grimnir's is battle. You can keep vigil at Valaya's hearth, or go to Grimnir's shrine and swear an oath on your axe.
Valaya's hearth.
Grimnir's shrine.
You come back from the shrine changed. The ancestors were close, closer than they have been in years, and you think they were pleased with you.
Thanks be to the ancestors.
Valaya's Blessing
This runesmith has kept vigil at Valaya's hearth.
Oath to Grimnir
This runesmith has sworn an oath on his axe at Grimnir's shrine.

It has been a long time since the runesmiths of the Guild worked together at one forge. A Runemoot: a gathering of masters, each with their own lore, to strike one great work that none of them could make alone. Your forge is fit for it. But runesmiths are a proud and quarrelsome lot, and the Guild still talks about the last moot that ended in a brawl.
Send out the summons.
Call a §YRunemoot§! at your forge.
Not now.
The summons go out, and the answers come back. [great_minds_guest_1.GetTitledFirstName] will come as guest of honour, and [great_minds_guest_2.GetTitledFirstName] as well. Others have been asked.
Make ready the forge.

[From.GetTitledFirstName] writes back: "I will come, gladly. But I would bring [great_minds_guest_4.GetTitledFirstName] with me. There is no better smith in my hold."\n\nYou and [great_minds_guest_4.GetFirstName] do not get on, and [From.GetFirstName] knows it.
Write a polite excuse.
Turn [great_minds_guest_4.GetFirstName] away politely. It may still give offence.
Very well, they may both come.
Both come to the moot.
Come, but not with [great_minds_guest_4.GetFirstName].
A plain refusal is a §Rscandal§!.
Then neither of you need come.
Turning away a guest is a §Rscandal§!.

The guests are gathered at your anvil, and the ale has gone round twice. Now you must say what the moot will forge. A work of war, for the hold's warriors. A work for the hold's wealth, for its mines and halls. Or a work of lore, for the Guild itself.
A work of war.
Forge a §Ywork of war§!.
A work for the hold's wealth.
Forge a §Ywork of wealth§!.
A work of lore.
Forge a §Ywork of lore§!.
[From.GetTitledFirstName] slams a mug on the bench. "Is that what we came all this way for? Any clan smith could make that. I say we forge something worthy of us."\n\nThe others look at you.
Argue it out.
A shouting contest, a Rorkaz, with [From.GetFirstName].
If you win, your work is forged.
If you lose, [From.GetFirstName]'s work is forged and you lose face.
Very well, we do it your way.
[From.GetFirstName]'s work is forged.
This is my forge. We do it my way.
Overruling a guest at the moot is a §Rscandal§!.
No one objects. For once, a room full of runesmiths agrees on something. It may be the ale.
Then to work.
The work begins.
The Rorkaz goes on until the lamps burn low. At last [FromFrom.GetFirstName] runs out of breath and sits down, red in the face. You have won.
To work, then.
The Rorkaz goes on until the lamps burn low, and at the end of it the others are nodding at [FromFrom.GetFirstName], not at you. You have lost, in your own forge.
We do it their way.
The guest's work is forged.

The work has begun, and already [great_minds_guest_1.GetFirstName] and [great_minds_guest_2.GetFirstName] are at odds. [great_minds_guest_1.GetFirstName] wants to try a binding no smith has struck before. [great_minds_guest_2.GetFirstName] says the old runes are good enough for the ancestors and good enough for us, and anything new is Grobkaz.
The old way. The runes the ancestors taught.
Keep to the old runes: §Ysafer§!, but the work will be less great.
Something new.
Try something new: a §Ygreater§! work if it holds, a §Rdisaster§! if it does not.

It has come to shouting. [arguer_1.GetFirstName] says [arguer_2.GetFirstName] struck a rune crooked on purpose, and [arguer_2.GetFirstName] says [arguer_1.GetFirstName] could not strike a straight rune if Thungni guided the hammer. Their hands are on their axes.
Step between them.
Try to make peace.
If you succeed, the work goes on.
If you fail, it gets worse.
Send [arguer_1.GetFirstName] home.
Sending a guest home is a §Rscandal§!.
Send [arguer_2.GetFirstName] home.
Sending a guest home is a §Rscandal§!.
You get them to sit down, and to drink, and in the end to shake hands. They will not be friends. But they will work.
Back to the anvil.
The quarrel is over.
You step between them, and [arguer_1.GetFirstName] shoves you aside. Now there is a grudge to write down, and everyone saw it.
This moot is going badly.
The quarrel becomes a §Rscandal§!.

You and [From.GetFirstName] fall into the rhythm of the work without a word, one hammer striking as the other lifts, the way smiths work who have worked together all their lives. You never had before.
Another mug, when we are done.
Late in the night, alone at your anvil with the work in front of you, you see it. All of it, the whole shape of the binding, every rune in its place. Your hands are shaking.
Wake the others. Now.
Your insight will make the work greater.
It is finished: a great hammer of gromril, its head struck with runes by every master at the moot, each of them adding their own. When you lift it, the forge goes quiet.

It is finished: a lodestone set in gromril and struck with runes of finding, that points the miners to the richest seam and never errs. The mine-masters of the hold come to see it, and leave talking about nothing else.

It is finished: a great tablet of stone, not of runes, for the Guild writes none down, but of the Rules and the tallies and the names of the masters, struck by every smith at the moot. It will be the pride of the Guild's halls.
It is finished: plans for a great bolt thrower, and a first one built, its bolts struck with runes of piercing. The engineers will grumble that the runesmiths are doing their work.
It is finished: a furnace for the hold's smelters, struck with runes of heat, that burns hotter than any in the hold. The smelters will have more iron than they know what to do with.

It is finished: a rune cipher, a way of striking messages in runes that only a runesmith of the Guild can read. Grudges, debts, the names of traitors: none of it will ever be read by Umgi or grobi again.
It is finished: a suit of gromril armour, its plates struck with runes of warding. It is not the greatest work ever made at a moot, but it is very good.
It is finished: a set of rune-struck millstones for the hold's mills, that grind faster and never wear. A useful thing, if not a glorious one.
It is finished: a pair of rune-struck spectacles that let an old runesmith see a rune as clearly as he did when he was young. The Full Beards of the Guild are very pleased.
A hammer the ancestors would be proud of.
The mines will be rich.
Let it stand in the Guild's halls.
Let the grobi come.
The smelters will be glad.
Let our enemies try to read it.
Good, honest work.
Bread is bread.
My old eyes thank you.
The work does not hold. The runes will not bind, however many times you strike them, and in the end the masters set down their hammers and admit it. All that labour, and nothing to show for it.
The binding goes wrong. There is a flash, and a noise like the mountain cracking, and then smoke and screaming. When it clears, the anvil is split and not everyone at the moot is still standing.
Kruk.
The moot ends with §Ynothing forged§!.
Krunk.
The blast may §Rmaim or kill§! you and your guests.
One quarrel too many. The guests gather their tools and leave, one by one, and the last of them spits on your threshold on the way out. The Guild will be talking about this moot for a hundred years.
Write them all in the book of grudges.
The moot is over, and §Rnothing§! was forged.

Your store is running low. A rune can only be as good as what it is struck into, and the salves that bind it go bad if they are kept too long. You will need new ore and fresh salve before you strike again, and [gathering_companion.GetFirstName] can come with you to carry it.\n\nThe old workings below the hold are worked out for iron, but the deep seams still give up the stuff runesmiths want, if you know where to look. Or there are the traders' halls, where the clans sell what they dig.

[gathering_companion.GetTitledFirstName] is waiting with a lamp and two empty sacks. "The Guild wants fresh ore and fresh salve, and it wants them soon. We go together. Down the workings, or to the traders?"
Down the old workings.
Go looking for ore and §Yrune salves§! in the old workings. Good §Ystewardship§! helps.
To the traders' halls.
Go buying §Yrunic metals§! in the traders' halls. Good §Ydiplomacy§! helps, and it costs gold.
Not now.

[From.GetTitledFirstName] has been through your store and does not like what [From.GetSheHe] found. "Half your salve has gone to crust and there is more rust than ore in here. Get yourself fresh stock, [Root.GetFirstName], before you shame the Guild with a rune that will not hold."

The old workings go down further than anyone remembers. The miners' marks on the walls are worn almost smooth, and in places they point to tunnels that fell in long ago. Somewhere down here there are seams the miners never finished, and the stuff in them is what a runesmith's salves are made of.
Follow the old miners' marks.
Tap the walls and listen to the rock.
Dig wherever it looks promising.
You come up out of the workings filthy, bruised and grinning, with both sacks full. [From.GetFirstName] found a seam the miners missed, and there is enough in it for salves to last you a long while.
Weeks in the dark for a few handfuls of what you came for. It will do, for now.
Kruk. Weeks in the workings and nothing to show for them but bruises. Then a roof that had held for a thousand years chose that day to come down.
A rich haul.
You gain §Yrune salves§!.
Something, at least.
Grungni, why?

The traders' halls are loud with haggling. Every clan in the hold sells here, and every one of them swears its ore is the purest and its price the fairest. Most of them are lying. Some of them owe your clan a favour from long ago, if anyone remembers.
Remind them of the old debts between our clans.
Buy the traders a round, and then talk.
Pay what they ask.
A cart full of good metal, at a price you will not have to be ashamed of. [From.GetFirstName] haggled like a Longbeard.
A few good ingots, and a lot of talk. Your purse is lighter, but so is it always.
Umgak, all of it. The ingots you bought crumble under the first blow of the hammer. You have been robbed, and in the hold's own halls.
A full cart.
A few ingots.
Write the trader's name in the book of grudges.
Gather Ore and Salves
A runesmith's store must be kept full of fresh ore and salve.
Go down the old workings or to the traders' halls, and come back with a good haul.

[From.GetTitledFirstName] has a commission for you. "Runesmiths seldom sell their work, and this is no sale. [client_target.GetTitledFirstName] has asked the Guild for a piece, and the Guild has named you. It is an honour, apprentice or no. You have a year."

[From.GetTitledFirstName] has a commission for you. "[client_target.GetTitledFirstName] has asked the Guild for a piece of runesmith's work, and has the leave of the Runelord for it. The Guild has named you. You have a year. Do not make us regret it."
You have a year to deliver the work.
A letter from the Guild:\n\n"A year has passed, and [Root.GetTitledFirstName] has delivered nothing. The Guild's word was given, and [Root.GetSheHe] has broken it. This will be remembered."
Kruk.
[client_target.GetTitledFirstName] wants a weapon: an axe or a hammer, made by a runesmith, fit to be handed down to grandsons.
[client_target.GetTitledFirstName] wants armour, made by a runesmith, that will turn a troll's club.
[client_target.GetTitledFirstName] wants a rune, struck by a runesmith of the Guild, to be set into a weapon of the clan.
I have good metal for a weapon.
I have no metal to make a weapon with.
I have good metal for armour.
I have no metal to make armour with.
I have the salve to bind a rune.
I have no salve to bind a rune with.
Gromril. Only the best.
The blade is roughed out on your anvil, still glowing. Now comes the long work.
The plates are cut and the rivets laid out on the bench. Now comes the long work.
The salve is warm and the chisel sharp. Now comes the long work: a rune must be struck right the first time, or not at all.
Honest work for an honest price.
Every blow counted. It will take as long as it takes.
The work may become a §Gmasterwork§!.
It is finished, and it is good work. [client_target.GetTitledFirstName] has sent a cart to collect it.
It is finished, and it is the best thing you have ever made. You find you do not want to let it go. [client_target.GetTitledFirstName] has sent a cart to collect it.
Load the cart.
Send the cart back empty. It is mine.
A Commission for
A dwarf lord has asked the Guild for a piece of runesmith's work, and the Guild has named you.

§Gright-click§! the portrait of your client and choose §YBegin Crafting§!. You need §Yore§! for weapons and armour or §Ysalve§! for a rune. Deliver the work within a year for §Y[Root.Society.GetCurrency]§!. Keep it, or fail, and the Guild will §Rstrip your standing§!.

Every anvil has its purpose, the old masters say, as the ancestors' own anvils did. You have struck runes of every kind, but a Runelord must choose the lore he will give his life to. Valaya's anvil is the hearth, the home and the warding rune. Grimnir's is battle. Grungni's is labour and protection, the mine and the wall. Thungni's is the rune itself.
Valaya: the hearth and the ward.
Grimnir: the axe and the battle.
Grungni: the mine and the wall.
Thungni: the rune itself.
Tablet of the Guild

A great tablet struck by the masters of a Runemoot. It holds no runes, for the Guild writes none down, but the Rules of Three, of Form, of Jealousy and of Pride, and the names and tallies of the masters who struck it.
The masons begin cutting your §Yforge§!.
You must have §Yore§! or §Ysalve§! in your store.
You must not already be working on a commission.
§Y[From.GetTitledFirstName]§! has a commission to forge a piece for §Y[Root.GetTitledFirstName]§!.
Study a Gromdal
Every rune a smith of the ancestors struck carries his mark, and in the mark is how he struck it. Study a gromdal, a work of the ancestors, and learn what its smith knew.
Has NOT studied a gromdal in the last five years
Choose a §Ygromdal§! to study.

Nothing the Guild knows is written down, but the ancestors left something better than writing: their work. Every rune a master struck carries his mark, and a runesmith with the patience to read it can learn how the stroke was made, how deep, at what angle, with what chant.\n\nThere is the gromdal of your own clan in the hall, an axe your forefathers have carried for generations. [runesmith_mark_owner.GetTitledFirstName] keeps an older one and might lend it to you. And in the grave-hall below the hold lie the oldest of all, with their smiths, under the eyes of the priests.
My own clan's heirloom.
Your own clan's piece: §Ysafe§!, but you may know it too well to see anything new.
Ask [runesmith_mark_owner.GetFirstName] to lend me theirs.
Another clan's piece. Its runes are not yours to take: the §YRule of Jealousy§! holds.
Go down to the grave-hall.
The oldest pieces say the most, but the dead do not like to be disturbed.
Not now.

Weeks with a lamp and a lens, tracing each stroke with a fingertip, and then one night it opens to you all at once. You can see the smith at his anvil, the hammer rising and falling, the chant on his breath. You know how this rune was struck. You could strike it yourself.

The mark gives up most of its secrets. Not all: there is a stroke near the end you cannot follow, and you suspect you never will. But you have learned more in these months than in years at your own anvil.
A little. You see now why the smith angled one stroke as he did, and that alone was worth the looking.
The marks mean nothing to you. You stare at them until your eyes burn, and they stay what they were: scratches on old iron.
Keep the knowledge, and honour the smith who struck it.
Strike his rune into a work of my own.
The rune belongs to another clan's smith. Striking it breaks the §RRule of Jealousy§!.
It was worth the looking.
The mark keeps its secrets.

As you climb the stair out of the grave-hall, something stirs behind you. A warding rune, cut into the lintel of the tomb by a smith dead two thousand years, has woken. It knows you were here, and that you went away with nothing.
Ancestors, forgive me.
Reader of Old Marks
This runesmith has learned from the mark of an ancestor's work.
Studied a Gromdal

Nothing the Guild knows is written down, but the ancestors left something better than writing: their work. Every rune a master struck carries his mark, and a runesmith with the patience to read it can learn how the stroke was made, how deep, at what angle, with what chant.\n\nThere is the gromdal of your own clan in the hall, an axe your forefathers have carried for generations. And in the grave-hall below the hold lie the oldest of all, with their smiths, under the eyes of the priests.
ENGLISH

column1: # Engineers Guild events and decisions (events/WHG_engineer_events.txt, decisions/WHG_engineer_decisions.txt)

column2: The Engineers Guild

The most secretive of the Dawi craft guilds. Its clans honour Grungni and Morgrim, the First Engineer, and its heart is the great crafts halls of Zhufbar. Black powder, cannon, handguns, the gyrocopter and the steam borer are its works, and the Elders of the guild trust nothing new until it has been tested a hundred years.\n\nThe guild has three homes. The Dawi keep its secrets in the holds, and the Imperial Dwarf clans of the manling cities sell its craft to manlings, never its runes, and pay a tithe to Zhufbar for the right. The §YImperial Gunnery School§! of Nuln was built by Dawi engineers cast out for radical ideas, and it still pays the guild its due. The §YImperial Engineers School§! of Altdorf, founded by a Tilean genius, is the manlings' own, and forever envious of both.
The Guildmaster of the Engineers Guild, first among its Elders.
Apprentice
Journeyman
Master Engineer
Guild Elder
Apprentice
Journeyman
Master Engineer
Guild Elder
Craftsmanship

An Imperial manling may join through the §YImperial Gunnery School§! while it stands in Nuln and Nuln is in Imperial hands, or through the §YImperial Engineers School§! once it has been open in Altdorf for a year.

A letter sealed with the guild's mark, a cogwheel struck over Morgrim's anvil:\n\n"[Root.GetFirstName], the Elders have weighed you and found you sound. You may enter the crafts halls as an apprentice. What you are shown there you will show no one outside the guild, not your clan, not your king. Break that oath and the guild will know, and the guild does not forgive."

A letter sealed with the guild's mark, a cogwheel struck over an anvil:\n\n"[Root.GetFirstName], the masters of Nuln have spoken for you, and the Elders have let it stand. You may enter the guild as an apprentice. Know that few manlings have been shown what you will be shown, and that many in the holds think none should be. Keep the guild's secrets as a Dawi would, and prove them wrong."
I will keep the guild's secrets.

The drawings have covered your bench for months. Gears, valves, a boiler no bigger than a helm, a firing chamber the guild's books say cannot be made that small. You have built it anyway, piece by piece, in a corner of the crafts hall where the Elders do not often look.\n\nNow it sits on the testing ground, hissing quietly. There is only one way to find out if it works.
Light the boiler.
It may work, it may not, it may blow up. §YLearning§!, a steady hand and a §YDwarf Engineer§!'s training make it less likely to blow up.

There is a noise like a cannon going off inside a barrel, and then you are on your back, ears ringing, looking up at a sky full of smoke and falling bits of brass. Someone is shouting. It might be you.\n\nThe Elders will have a great deal to say about this. At least you have learned what not to do.
Write down what went wrong. If I can still write.

It hisses. It rattles. It shakes itself half off the bench and then stops, with a sad little cough of steam. You try again the next day, and the day after. It will not work. Somewhere in the drawings there is a mistake, and you cannot find it.
Back to the drawings.

It works. Not a wonder, nothing to shake the holds, but it does what you meant it to do and it does it every time. The miners will want one. So will the brewers. Even the Elders grunt something that might be approval, which from them is near enough a feast.
Good, honest work.

It works better than you ever dreamed. It is brilliant. And the Elders, having watched it run, have ordered it locked in the guild's vaults, untried and unproven, until such time as it has been tested properly. By which they mean in a century or two.\n\nThe guild does not change its ways for one bright engineer. But the guild has seen what you can do, and it will remember.
In a hundred years they will thank me.

Three years of work, and it is finished. The whole crafts hall has stopped to watch it run: Elders, masters, apprentices with their mouths open. It does what no engine of the guild has done before, and it does it without a single bolt out of place.\n\nNo one says it is too new. Not even the oldest of the Elders. They put their hands on it, one by one, as their grandfathers once put their hands on Morgrim's first cannon.
Morgrim himself would not be ashamed of this.

The Elders gather in the oldest of the crafts halls, under the great cogwheel of Morgrim. One by one they look over the work you have brought them, and one by one they put their marks to it. You are a Master Engineer of the guild. There are holds that have not seen one in a generation.

Your master hands you a set of tools: hammers, gauges, a spanner of your own, each one marked with your name and the guild's cog. "You have learned what an apprentice can learn," [Root.GetSheHe] is told. "Now you are an engineer of the Dawi. Do not shame the tools."

The masters of the guild have watched you for years, and they have decided. You are given a guild engineer's tools and the right to work in the crafts halls without a master at your shoulder. Not many manlings have been given as much. Some of the Dawi will never accept it, but the tools are yours.
I will make good use of them.

You have spent more years at the bench than most manlings live, and there is little left in the guild's books you have not read, built and taken apart again. The Elders have noticed. A message comes from the crafts halls: you are to be named a Master Engineer, by the long work of your hands.
It is about time.

A guild messenger finds you with a letter from Zhufbar. The Elders have heard of you: a sharp mind, a good hand, a head that asks how things work. They offer you a place as an apprentice in the crafts halls of Zhufbar, the greatest in the Karaz Ankor, where the river turns the guild's wheels and the forges never go cold.\n\nIt is an honour few of the young are given. It would also mean years away from home.
Zhufbar it is.
My clan needs me here.
Word comes from Zhufbar: [From.GetFirstName] has been taken in by the Engineers Guild as an apprentice. The whole clan will hear of it, and so will the clans who sneered at yours.
Make us proud.

[From.GetTitledFirstName] has come to Zhufbar to learn the engineer's craft. The guild has room for [From.GetHerHim] in the crafts halls, and [From.GetSheHe] has asked, as is the custom, to take service in your hold while [From.GetSheHe] learns.
Welcome. There is a lot to build.
Let [From.GetHerHim] study, and then go home.

A grey-bearded Dawi arrives at your gate with a cart of tools, a crate of drawings and a very low opinion of your walls. The Engineers Guild has sent [engineer_hired.GetFirstName] of Zhufbar to serve you. [engineer_hired.GetSheHe] has already started making a list of what needs fixing.
Welcome, master engineer.

The school's halls rise above the Reik, with its foundry, its proving grounds and its library of drawings. All that is missing is someone to lead it. The Empire has relied on Dawi engineers for centuries, and has never yet made its own. That is what the school is for.\n\nTwo names are put forward. A Tilean genius, the kind of man who sketches flying machines in the margins of his letters. Or a Dawi master of the Nuln clans, who has worked beside Imperial gunners all his long life, and who knows the guild's ways from the inside.
The Tilean. Let the school be bold.
The Dawi master. Let the school be sound.
Test a New Device
Enough copying the old masters' drawings. You have built something new, and it is time to find out if it works.
Test a new device of your own. It may help the realm, prove ahead of its time, or blow up.
You test your new device.
You have not tested a device in the last §Y2 years§!.
Become an Engineer
You have served your time as an apprentice. Ask the masters to judge your work and give you an engineer's tools.
Gain the §YDwarf Engineer§! trait, or §YEngineer§! for a manling.
Engineering Improvements
Put the guild's knowledge to work at your capital: cranes, pulleys, better mortar, proper drains.
Building at your capital is cheaper and quicker for 5 years.
Engineering Improvements
The guild's engineers are at work here, and buildings go up cheaper and faster.
Call Up Thunderers
The guild keeps handguns in its armouries for the day they are needed. That day has come.
At war, raise a regiment of Thunderers at your capital. They go home when the war ends.
A regiment of §Y300§! Thunderers musters at your capital. It disbands when the war ends.
You have not called on the guild's armouries in the last §Y5 years§!.
Roll Out the War Machines
Every master engineer keeps a few machines under tarpaulin for times like these. Bring out the cannon.
At war, raise a battery of cannon with Thunderers to guard it at your capital. They go home when the war ends.
A battery of §Y30§! cannon and §Y200§! Thunderers musters at your capital. It disbands when the war ends.
Become a Master Engineer
Bring your life's work before the Elders and ask to be named a Master Engineer of the guild.
A §YDwarf Engineer§! with §Y18§! learning may become a §YDwarf Engineering Master§!.
Begin a Masterwork
Clear the great crafts hall and start the work of a lifetime. It will take three years, and it may be the greatest engine the guild has ever made.
Spend three years on a masterwork. It may advance the realm's knowledge, and once in a lifetime it may become a treasure of the guild.
You spend the next §Y3 years§! on your masterwork.
Hire an Engineer
Ask the Engineers Guild to send one of its engineers from Zhufbar to serve at your court.
A §YDwarf Engineer§! of Zhufbar joins your court.
You have not hired an engineer in the last §Y10 years§!.
Found the Imperial Engineers School

For centuries the Empire has bought its cannon and its engineers from the Dawi. The Prince of Altdorf can pay for a school of the Empire's own, and there is a Tilean genius in the city who would gladly run it.
The §YImperial Engineers School§! opens in Altdorf and is added to the city's great works. A year later, Imperial manlings may join the §YEngineers Guild§! through it.
Recently Tested a Device
This engineer tested a new device not long ago.
Called on the Guild's Armouries
This lord has recently raised troops from the Engineers Guild.
Hired an Engineer
This ruler has recently hired an engineer from the guild.
Working on a Masterwork
This engineer is busy with a masterwork and has no time for anything else.
Practical Innovation
This engineer's latest device works, and folk can use it today.
Impractical Innovation
This engineer's latest device is no use to anyone, at least for now.
Masterwork of the Guild

An engine of brass and steel, made in the crafts halls by a Guild Elder over three years. Every gear and valve bears the guild's mark, and the Elders themselves put their hands on it the day it first ran.
Hire a Manling Engineer

Hire an engineer of the Imperial Engineers School in Altdorf, or one of Tilea's own inventors, for your court. They are not Dawi, and the Dawi will tell you so, but they are cheaper and far more willing to try something new.
A manling §YEngineer§! joins your court: a Tilean master, a graduate of the §YImperial Engineers School§! if it is open, or else a gunner of the §YGunnery School§! of Nuln.
Commission a War Machine
Set your court's engineer to building war machines at your capital: a battery of great cannon, or, for an Imperial court once the Imperial school is open, one of its famous Steam Tanks.
No war machine is being built in your lands.
A battery of §Y20 great cannon§! joins your army at the capital.
A §YSteam Tank§! joins your army at the capital.
Casting Great Cannon
The court's engineer has the capital's foundries casting great cannon, and the workshops have little time for anything else.
Building a Steam Tank
The court's engineer is building a Steam Tank at the capital. Half the city's smiths are at work on its boiler.

[engineer_hired.GetFirstName] arrives from Miragliano with three carts of drawings, a working model of a flying machine and no fewer than four inventions he is sure will change the art of war. Tilea breeds such men. Not all of them are mad.

[engineer_hired.GetFirstName] arrives from the Imperial Engineers School in Altdorf, ink on his fingers and a slide rule in his coat. The school has sent its fee on ahead to the Prince of Altdorf, who keeps it. He asks first to see your foundries, and second where the nearest Dawi are, so that he can avoid them.
Welcome to my court.

Your engineer has cleared a workshop at the capital and spread his drawings across every table in it. The foundries are ready, he says. All he needs to know is what you want built, and how much gold you are willing to melt down to build it.
A battery of great cannon.
A Steam Tank.
Not now.

The last of the great cannon has been proved on the range outside the walls. None burst. Twenty barrels of the finest bronze stand in the yard, each with your arms cast into the breech, and the gun crews are already arguing over which one is the loudest.
The foundries have gone cold. With no engineer left at court to see the casting through, the half-finished cannon have been broken up for the bronze.
Magnificent.

Two years of hammering, three boiler explosions and one very singed engineer later, the Steam Tank rolls out of the workshop on its own steam, its bell clanging and its cannon swinging round to face the gate. The crowd that gathered to watch has backed away a good distance.
The Steam Tank stands half-built in the workshop and will never move. With no engineer left at court, nobody understands the drawings well enough to finish it.
What a wonderful machine.
Engineer of the Holds
This Dawi works in the crafts halls of the holds, under the eye of the Elders of Zhufbar. The Dawi of the holds build the deep works and the forts, and they build them to last.
Engineer of the Manling Cities

This Dawi works among manlings, in the Dwarf quarters of Nuln, Altdorf and the other cities of men. The Imperial Dwarf clans sell the guild's craft to manlings, never its runes, and pay a tithe to Zhufbar for the right. The holds have never quite forgiven them.
Imperial Engineers School

This engineer belongs to the manling tradition of Tilea and the Imperial Engineers School of Altdorf, founded by Leonardo of Miragliano. Its masters build Steam Tanks, flying machines and things that have no names yet, and the Dawi think most of them are mad.
Imperial Gunnery School

This engineer was trained at the Imperial Gunnery School of Nuln, behind eighteen feet of soot-black limestone above the Aver. The School casts the Empire's cannon, mortars and Hellblaster Volley Guns, and trains the gunners who serve them.

Two letters lie on the table. One bears the seal of the Imperial Engineers School of Altdorf, with a cramped hand promising a bench in the workshops where the Steam Tanks are built. The other is from the Council of Masters of the Gunnery School of Nuln, offering a place among the gunners, smiths and engineers of the Empire's great foundry.\n\nThe two schools do not like each other. You can belong to only one.
Altdorf. I want to build what has never been built.
Nuln. I want to make the guns that win wars.

An apprentice of the hold has built something the guild's books do not know: a valve that opens itself when the boiler runs too hot. It works. That is not the point, say the Elders. It is new, it has not been tested a hundred years, and the books do not know it. They want it broken up and the drawings burned, and they want you to do it.
The Elders are right. Break it up.
It works. Let him test it.

The steam borer is set to the rock face of a new seam, deep under the hold. It shrieks like a dragon and shakes the gallery to its roots. The miners have stepped back. At full pressure it would cut through in a week. At full pressure, it might also bring the roof down.
Full pressure. Drive it through.
Slow and careful, as the Elders taught.

The collector from Zhufbar stands at your door, an old Dawi with a ledger under his arm and the patience of stone. The Dawi of the manling cities pay the guild a tithe for the right to sell its craft to manlings. Yours is due. He has come a long way, and he does not intend to go back without it.
Pay it, to the last penny.
Tell him it will come with the next caravan.

A manling apprentice has been staring at the marks on a Dawi gun for an hour. At last he works up the nerve to ask: what do they mean? Do they make it shoot further? Could he learn them?\n\nThe guild lets manlings learn the craft. It has never let them learn the runes, and the runes are not even the guild's to give.
Runes are not for manlings.
Tell him a little. Only a little.

A new gun is set to cool, and the Silence Bells ring out over the Industrialplatz. For an hour Nuln goes quiet. The carts stop, the hammers stop, business is done in whispers, for every gunner knows that a loud noise can put a flaw in cooling metal. But the war will not wait an hour, and the drills are already behind.
Keep the silence.
There is a war on. Keep the drills going.

The gunnery season is over, and the last of the year's powder is getting old and unstable. So the Sons of the Guns stand at the gates of the Gunnery School at noon with baskets of firecrackers, sparklers and smoke bombs, and hand them out to anyone who asks. It is Black Powder Week, and half of Nuln is in the streets.
Hand them out myself.
Keep the powder in the stores.

The Gunnery School takes in Nuln's orphan boys and teaches them a trade, and in return they work its forges before dawn. One of these Sons of the Guns has caught your eye: quick with figures, steady at the gun, and up an hour before anyone else. His debt to the school is large. Someone could pay it, and take him into service.
Pay his way and take him into service.
The school will see to him.

A pamphlet from Nuln is going round Altdorf's taverns. It shows the Engineers School's newest machine with its boiler on fire and its inventor running, and underneath it says: "Altdorf builds them, Nuln buries them." The masters of the school want an answer.
Answer in print, and sharper.
Write to Nuln's masters and mend it.

In the school's archive is a drawing in Leonardo's mirror hand: wings of oiled canvas on a frame of ash, a seat, and a pedal crank. Some student has built it, and it stands on the roof of the school above the Reik. Nobody has yet been brave enough, or foolish enough, to sit in it.
Climb in. Someone must.
Sell the drawing to a Tilean.
Petition the Elders
Put a new design before the Elders of the guild at Zhufbar. If they approve it, the guild will honour you. If not, they will tell you so, at length.
§YEngineers of the Holds§! may put a design before the Elders of Zhufbar.
In a month the Elders give their verdict. A §YMaster Engineer§!, high §YLearning§! and a stubborn beard make them likelier to approve. Radical ideas make them less likely.
You have petitioned the Elders in the last five years.
Teach the Manlings
Teach the ablest manling at your court, or your lord's, the guild's craft. Not one rune. The guild takes its tithe.
§YEngineers of the Manling Cities§! may teach a manling the craft.
The ablest manling of learning 8 or more at your court, or your liege's, becomes an §YEngineer§!. The tithe goes to the lord of §YZhufbar§!.
There is a manling of learning 8 or more, not yet an engineer, at your court or your liege's.
You have taken a manling pupil in the last five years.
Christen a Gun
A new gun has been cast for you at Nuln. Send its name to be cut into the barrel, and watch the Guildmaster pour the sacred oil. Which way it runs foretells the gun's fate.
§YGunnery School§! rulers may christen a new gun of Nuln.
The oil foretells a siege gun, a battle gun or, rarely, disaster.
You have christened a gun in the last five years.
If the oil runs right, a great siege gun. If it runs left, a gun ferocious in battle. If it pools on the barrel, disaster. High §YLearning§! and an §YEngineer§!'s eye make disaster less likely.
Study Leonardo's Notebooks
Spend two years with the notebooks Leonardo of Miragliano left the school, written backwards and half in cipher.
§YEngineers School§! masters may study Leonardo's notebooks.
In two years you learn what you can. Once in a lifetime, the notebooks may give up a secret for good.
You become an §YEngineer of the Manling Cities§!. If you are not a ruler, you go to the court of the lord of §YNuln§!.

The Elders of Zhufbar have had your drawings for a month. They have turned them over, measured them, argued over them, and sent for the oldest books in the guild's vaults to see if anything like it was ever made before. At last the eldest of them grunts and says: "It will do." From the Elders of the Engineers Guild, there is no higher praise.
It will do.

The Elders give your drawings back unread past the second page. "New," says the eldest, as other Dawi say "Grobi." The design is not to be built. If you value your place in the guild, you will forget it.\n\nIt was such Dawi, cast out for radical ideas, who went to the manlings and built the guns of Nuln. Some say they were the guild's shame. Some say they were its future.
I bow to the Elders.
Then I will take it to the manling cities.

[engineer_pupil.GetTitledFirstName] has a quick mind for a manling, and a patient one, which is rarer. You show [engineer_pupil.GetHerHim] the craft as the guild allows: the casting, the boring, the mixing of the powder. When [engineer_pupil.GetSheHe] asks about the runes on your hammer, you change the subject.
The craft, and not one rune.

The gun lies on its trestles in the foundry yard, still dark from the mould, with the name you sent cut into its barrel. The masters of the Mechanics Guild stand round it in their best coats. The Guildmaster comes forward with the flask of sacred oil and lets a little dribble onto the barrel. Everyone leans in to see which way it runs.
Watch the oil.
The oil runs down the right side of the barrel. A siege gun, then, say the masters, the kind that brings down walls. The gunners are already arguing over which city it will be.
Let the walls of my enemies beware.
The oil runs down the left side of the barrel. A battle gun, say the masters, the kind that sends many foes to their end. The crew grin at each other.
Let the armies of my enemies beware.

The oil does not run. It pools on top of the barrel and sits there, gleaming. Nobody speaks. Every gunner in Nuln knows what that means: a flaw in the metal, and a gun that will one day burst and take its crew with it.
Melt it down.
Superstition. Send it to the front.

Two years in, a page you have read a hundred times turns over in your mind, and suddenly you can read it. Not the cipher: the thought behind it. You understand, for an hour, the way Leonardo of Miragliano looked at the world, and you see that he was right about things the school has not yet dared to build.
I see it now.

You have not cracked the cipher, but you have pieced together one design from the notebooks' margins: a war engine, a boiler and an iron shell on wheels, with a cannon in its nose. It is not a Steam Tank. It might be the grandfather of the next one.
Send a copy to the workshops.
Two years, and the cipher has beaten you. You know more about the habits of Leonardo's hand than any man living, and almost nothing about what he wrote. The notebooks go back on their shelf.
Another master will crack it.
A battery from Nuln: mortars, a Hellblaster and the crews (150 gold, one year).

The guns arrive on barges up the river: two squat mortars, a long-barrelled cannon and a Hellblaster Volley Gun, with crews trained at the Gunnery School to serve them. They fire a salute on the quay, as they would at Nuln, and every window in the street shakes.
The battery was cast at Nuln and paid for, but without a gunner of Nuln at court nobody knew how to receive it. The guns were sold on to another lord before they ever reached you.
Bring up the guns!
A battery of §Y25 Artillery§! and §Y100 Handgunners§! of Nuln joins your army for good, if a gunner of Nuln is still at court.

[engineer_hired.GetFirstName] comes from the Imperial Gunnery School of Nuln, soot under his fingernails and a burn scar on one wrist. The School has sent its fee on to the lord of Nuln, its patron. He asks first to see your guns, and second to see your powder stores, and is not happy with either.

The Iron Silence
